title: English Vocabulary 4 · Units 37–38
description: Advanced vocabulary for festivals, cultural commemoration and atmosphere, followed by linguistic terminology, word families, semantic nuance and expressive communication.
sourceNotice: Prepared for personal study based on the user-supplied book. Vocabulary targets, word families and usage distinctions were checked against the relevant teaching pages, exercises and answer key. Translations, notes and example sentences were freshly written; textbook passages, exercise prompts and illustrations are not reproduced.

audit.scope: Unit 37 teaching sections A–B, cultural-festival example, word-family table, exercises 37.1–37.2 and answer key; Unit 38 teaching sections A–C, linguistic terms, word formation, exercises 38.1–38.4 and answer key.
audit.pronunciation: Selective broad British IPA is supplied only where reasonably confident; other IPA fields are empty. The book’s technical terminology is preserved, including variation-sensitive matters such as the number of diphthongs across accents.
audit.languagePolicy: English is used in all learner-facing fields and metadata except pt, which uses Brazilian Portuguese.
audit.reviewMethod: Compared teaching pages and corresponding PDF page images with exercises and the printed answer key; independently wrote English examples and usage notes and Brazilian Portuguese translations. Performed JSON/schema, source metadata, ID uniqueness, origin labels and static word/sentence audio-target linting.
audit.limitations: No MP3 audio is included. Real VocabLab import, browser-dependent text-to-speech and speech-recognition behaviours were not tested. IPA is deliberately omitted where no entry-level transcription was confidently established.

units.title: Unit 37 — Festivals in their cultural context
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 37. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
units.category: Culture and society · festivals, commemorations and celebratory language
learningObjectives: Describe festivals, ceremonies and commemorations using accurate collocations and cultural vocabulary.
Choose celebration/celebratory, festivities/festive, spectacle/spectacular and renewal/renew correctly.
Differentiate lively, flamboyant, raucous, sombre and atmospheric when describing public events.
Explain cultural origins and symbolism with expressions such as trace back to, commemorate and symbolise.

sectionsChecked: A · Describing festivals, Mombasa example and noun–verb–adjective table
B · Festival connotations, cultural origins and commemorations

items.pt: acontecer em novembro; cair no mês de novembro
items.section: A · Festivals, culture and celebrations
items.example: The city's annual heritage festival falls in November, after the rainy season.
items.note: For recurring events, fall in plus a month or fall on plus a day/date describes when they take place.

items.section: A · Festivals, culture and celebrations
items.example: Local residents were encouraged to participate in the festivities rather than merely watch.
items.note: Participate in is the usual formal construction; festivities refers to the collective celebratory activities.

items.section: A · Festivals, culture and celebrations
items.example: This year's programme will feature traditional performances from several communities.
items.note: Feature means include something as a prominent part of an event or programme.

items.section: A · Festivals, culture and celebrations
items.example: The festival reflects the city's multicultural history and contemporary population.
items.note: Describes the presence or interaction of more than one cultural tradition.

items.section: A · Festivals, culture and celebrations
items.example: The organisers hope the joint performances will promote integration across neighbourhoods.
items.note: Promote integration is a formal collocation for encouraging inclusion and social connections.

items.section: A · Festivals, culture and celebrations
items.example: The centenary was marked by a celebration involving the entire university community.
items.note: Noun for an act or event celebrating something; related to celebrate and celebratory.

items.section: A · Festivals, culture and celebrations
items.example: The town will celebrate the completion of its restoration project with an outdoor concert.
items.note: Transitive verb: celebrate an event, achievement or anniversary.

items.section: A · Festivals, culture and celebrations
items.example: A celebratory atmosphere developed as the final results were announced.
items.note: Adjective describing an occasion, mood or action intended to celebrate something.

items.section: A · Festivals, culture and celebrations
items.example: An international literature festival brings writers to the city every spring.
items.note: A festival is the event; festivities are the activities associated with celebrating it.

items.section: A · Festivals, culture and celebrations
items.example: The festivities continued well into the evening after the formal ceremony ended.
items.note: Usually plural when referring collectively to celebrations and associated activities.

items.pt: festivo; alegre e próprio de comemoração
items.section: A · Festivals, culture and celebrations
items.example: Lanterns and music gave the market a festive atmosphere.
items.note: Common collocations include festive mood, festive atmosphere and festive season.

items.section: A · Festivals, culture and celebrations
items.example: A colourful parade drew thousands of spectators to the city centre.
items.note: Countable noun for an organised procession, often in celebration.

items.section: A · Festivals, culture and celebrations
items.example: Performers paraded through the streets in elaborate costumes.
items.note: Parade is also a verb; unlike the noun, it describes the action of moving ceremonially.

items.section: A · Festivals, culture and celebrations
items.example: The illuminated boats created a remarkable spectacle after sunset.
items.note: The noun describes an impressive sight or public display; distinct from the adjective spectacular.

items.section: A · Festivals, culture and celebrations
items.example: The spectacular fireworks display concluded the anniversary celebrations.
items.note: Adjective; not interchangeable with the noun spectacle.

items.section: A · Festivals, culture and celebrations
items.example: The families prepared a feast to welcome the returning musicians.
items.note: Usually a large, special meal associated with celebration.

items.pt: banquetes e muita comida; ato de festejar comendo
items.section: A · Festivals, culture and celebrations
items.example: Several days of feasting followed the wedding ceremony.
items.note: An uncountable activity noun related to the verb feast; not identical to one feast.

items.section: A · Festivals, culture and celebrations
items.example: The official ceremony took place before the public concert.
items.note: A formal event following established customs or procedures.

items.section: A · Festivals, culture and celebrations
items.example: The mayor wore ceremonial robes during the procession.
items.note: Adjective describing formal or ritual functions, rather than an everyday celebration.

items.section: A · Festivals, culture and celebrations
items.example: A ceremonial procession moved slowly through the old city.
items.note: A procession emphasises formal, ordered movement of people.

items.section: A · Festivals, culture and celebrations
items.example: The spring celebration represents a period of renewal for the community.
items.note: Abstract noun for a fresh beginning or restoration; particularly important for seasonal festivals.

items.section: A · Festivals, culture and celebrations
items.example: The annual gathering helps renew a sense of shared identity.
items.note: Verb form; renew confidence, hope, commitment or a relationship.

items.section: A · Festivals, culture and celebrations
items.example: The peaceful agreement brought renewed hope to families affected by the conflict.
items.note: Renewed is adjectival here and implies hope returning or becoming stronger.

items.pt: supersticioso; que acredita em presságios ou forças sobrenaturais
items.section: B · Cultural meanings and descriptive register
items.example: Some participants are superstitious about starting a journey on certain dates.
items.note: Describes beliefs in luck or supernatural influences not based on rational evidence; can sound critical.

items.section: B · Cultural meanings and descriptive register
items.example: The museum commissioned a new exhibition for its centenary.
items.note: A hundredth anniversary; British-English form also used for the anniversary celebration.

items.section: B · Cultural meanings and descriptive register
items.example: The town marked the bi-centenary of its founding with a public history project.
items.note: A two-hundredth anniversary; also written bicentenary.

items.section: B · Cultural meanings and descriptive register
items.example: The dancers wore flamboyant costumes decorated with feathers and bright fabric.
items.note: Strongly colourful or conspicuous; can describe appearance, behaviour or style.

items.section: B · Cultural meanings and descriptive register
items.example: Raucous cheering echoed through the square as the performers arrived.
items.note: Noisy and boisterous; often less approving than lively.

items.section: B · Cultural meanings and descriptive register
items.example: The remembrance service maintained a sombre atmosphere throughout.
items.note: British spelling; American spelling somber. Suggests seriousness or sadness, not festivity.

items.pt: cheio de atmosfera; evocativo; com clima marcante
items.section: B · Cultural meanings and descriptive register
items.example: The candlelit courtyard provided an atmospheric setting for the concert.
items.note: Describes a place or event that creates a strong, particular mood.

items.section: B · Cultural meanings and descriptive register
items.example: The ritual can be traced back to agricultural traditions from several centuries ago.
items.note: Common passive pattern be traced back to a period, event or origin.

items.pt: pagão; associado a crenças religiosas pré-cristãs
items.section: B · Cultural meanings and descriptive register
items.example: Researchers examined the pagan origins of the seasonal ceremonies.
items.note: Cultural-historical term; avoid using it as a general synonym for superstitious.

items.pt: homenagear; lembrar solenemente; comemorar um acontecimento histórico
items.section: B · Cultural meanings and descriptive register
items.example: A ceremony will commemorate those who lost their lives in the disaster.
items.note: Formal verb used for respectfully remembering an event or people.

items.pt: estar associado a; estar relacionado a
items.section: B · Cultural meanings and descriptive register
items.example: This particular dance is associated with the start of the harvest season.
items.note: The construction links a tradition with an idea, event or group.

items.pt: ser o foco de; constituir a principal atenção de
items.section: B · Cultural meanings and descriptive register
items.example: Traditional music will be the focus of this year's programme.
items.note: Focus is the central subject or object of attention.

items.section: B · Cultural meanings and descriptive register
items.example: The painted branches symbolise the return of life after winter.
items.note: British spelling; American English symbolize. Typically transitive.

items.section: B · Cultural meanings and descriptive register
items.example: The regional anniversary was declared a public holiday so that residents could attend.
items.note: A day officially designated as a holiday; not merely a private day off.

items.section: B · Cultural meanings and descriptive register
items.example: Performers arrived in traditional costume for the cultural procession.
items.note: Costume can mean traditional or theatrical clothing; context decides the sense.

items.pt: aniversário de um evento; data comemorativa
items.section: B · Cultural meanings and descriptive register
items.example: An exhibition opened on the anniversary of the town's liberation.
items.note: Annual return of a significant date; a centenary is one particular anniversary.

units.title: Unit 38 — Talking about language
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 38. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
units.category: Language and communication · linguistics, semantics, registers and expression
learningObjectives: Distinguish syntax, phonology, lexicon, orthography and morphology and their related technical terms.
Use the linguistic word families modality/modal, lexicon/lexical, orthography/orthographic and polysemy/polysemous.
Describe metaphor, language change, obsolete terms, registers and jargon accurately.
Contrast articulate, eloquent, succinct and inarticulate, and use idioms about being unable to speak or causing embarrassment.

sectionsChecked: A · Linguistic terms: syntax, phonology, lexicon, orthography and morphology
B · Semantic variation, word change and registers
Exercises 38.1–38.4, word formation table and relevant answer-key entries

items.pt: sintaxe; regras de estrutura e ordem das palavras
items.section: A · Linguistics: structure, sound and form
items.example: Researchers compared the syntax of the two languages to identify structural differences.
items.note: Specialist term for sentence grammar and word order, not simply the size of a vocabulary.

items.section: A · Linguistics: structure, sound and form
items.example: Word order can change the emphasis or meaning of a sentence.
items.note: A key component of syntax; its flexibility varies across languages.

items.pt: modalidade linguística; expressão de possibilidade ou obrigação
items.section: A · Linguistics: structure, sound and form
items.example: The lecturer compared how different languages express modality in requests.
items.note: Linguistic term for meanings such as necessity, permission and possibility.

items.pt: modal; relativo à expressão de possibilidade ou necessidade
items.section: A · Linguistics: structure, sound and form
items.example: The modal meaning changes when the speaker replaces must with might.
items.note: Adjective from modality, with a different stress pattern.

items.section: A · Linguistics: structure, sound and form
items.example: A modal verb may express obligation, probability or permission.
items.note: Examples in the source include must, could and should.

items.pt: fonologia; sistema sonoro de uma língua
items.section: A · Linguistics: structure, sound and form
items.example: The course covers phonology before moving on to connected speech.
items.note: Study of the sound system of a language; not identical to spelling or orthography.

items.section: A · Linguistics: structure, sound and form
items.example: Changing one phoneme may turn a word into a completely different word.
items.note: A sound category that can distinguish meaning; notation usually uses slashes.

items.pt: ditongo; combinação de vogais na mesma sílaba
items.section: A · Linguistics: structure, sound and form
items.example: The vowel in the English word face is realised as a diphthong in many accents.
items.note: A vowel sound that glides between positions within a syllable; counts vary by accent.

items.pt: entonação; padrão de altura da voz
items.section: A · Linguistics: structure, sound and form
items.example: The speaker's intonation made the apparently neutral statement sound sarcastic.
items.note: Pitch pattern in speech; studied alongside other aspects of phonology.

items.pt: léxico; conjunto de palavras de uma língua
items.section: A · Linguistics: structure, sound and form
items.example: The lexicon of modern English continues to expand as new technologies emerge.
items.note: Linguistic term for a language's vocabulary; distinct from syntax.

items.section: A · Linguistics: structure, sound and form
items.example: The report identified several lexical differences between the regional varieties.
items.note: Adjective related to lexicon; unlike orthographic, it concerns vocabulary and word choice.

items.section: A · Linguistics: structure, sound and form
items.example: The study examined how orthography affects early reading skills.
items.note: Refers to conventional spelling and writing systems, not pronunciation.

items.pt: ortográfico; relativo às convenções de escrita
items.section: A · Linguistics: structure, sound and form
items.example: The dictionaries use different orthographic conventions for borrowed words.
items.note: Adjective from orthography; the book flags a stress shift in this pair.

items.section: A · Linguistics: structure, sound and form
items.example: Linguists developed a practical alphabet for recording the language.
items.note: An alphabet uses characters associated with speech sounds; not all writing systems are alphabetic.

items.section: A · Linguistics: structure, sound and form
items.example: The digital archive could not display several characters from the original manuscript.
items.note: In writing systems, a character is a written sign or symbol; it may be a letter or another kind of sign.

items.section: A · Linguistics: structure, sound and form
items.example: A pictogram at the station indicated the location of the lifts.
items.note: A character representing something by means of a picture; contrast with an ideogram.

items.pt: ideograma; símbolo de uma ideia ou conceito
items.section: A · Linguistics: structure, sound and form
items.example: The researcher explained how the ideogram represented an abstract concept.
items.note: A character representing an idea rather than merely picturing an object; writing-system terminology is complex.

items.pt: morfologia; formação e estrutura das palavras
items.section: A · Linguistics: structure, sound and form
items.example: Morphology explains how prefixes and suffixes contribute to word meaning.
items.note: Linguistic study of word structure; not the same as syntax at sentence level.

items.pt: morfema; menor unidade com significado ou função gramatical
items.section: A · Linguistics: structure, sound and form
items.example: The word reusable contains more than one morpheme.
items.note: A minimal meaningful unit in word structure; a morpheme need not be an independent word.

items.section: B · Meaning, change and varieties of language
items.example: The adjective sharp is polysemous, with uses that extend beyond physical edges.
items.note: Related meanings belong to the same word; do not confuse with different unrelated homonyms.

items.section: B · Meaning, change and varieties of language
items.example: The article explores the polysemy of words used to describe emotions.
items.note: Abstract noun corresponding to polysemous; noun and adjective keep the main stress in the book's table.

items.pt: contexto; palavras e circunstâncias ao redor de uma expressão
items.section: B · Meaning, change and varieties of language
items.example: Without context, it is difficult to know which interpretation the speaker intended.
items.note: Includes surrounding text and situation; a context can resolve ambiguity.

items.section: B · Meaning, change and varieties of language
items.example: The politician used a metaphor to describe the fragile economic recovery.
items.note: An expression understood figuratively rather than strictly literally.

items.section: B · Meaning, change and varieties of language
items.example: She used metaphorical language to describe the pressure of examinations.
items.note: The adjective from metaphor; the book notes a change in stress.

items.section: B · Meaning, change and varieties of language
items.example: After reviewing the data, the committee finally saw the light and revised its decision.
items.note: A figurative expression meaning understand or realise something; distinct from literal vision.

items.pt: uso da língua; formas de empregar palavras e construções
items.section: B · Meaning, change and varieties of language
items.example: A historical corpus can reveal changes in language usage over time.
items.note: Usage concerns how expressions are actually employed in speech or writing.

items.section: B · Meaning, change and varieties of language
items.example: Several terms in the eighteenth-century document are now obsolete.
items.note: For language, no longer ordinarily used; also describes outdated objects or systems.

items.section: B · Meaning, change and varieties of language
items.example: Journalists sometimes coin a word that quickly spreads through social media.
items.note: Coin is used figuratively to mean invent a new word or expression.

items.pt: registro linguístico; nível de formalidade e estilo de linguagem
items.section: B · Meaning, change and varieties of language
items.example: The email's formal register was appropriate for an official complaint.
items.note: A variety of language suited to a situation or audience; differs from specialist jargon.

items.pt: jargão; linguagem especializada de um grupo
items.section: B · Meaning, change and varieties of language
items.example: The manual was full of engineering jargon unfamiliar to new staff.
items.note: Terms shared by an occupation or interest group; can be necessary or unnecessarily obscure.

items.section: B · Meaning, change and varieties of language
items.example: The presenter translated computer jargon into terms that a general audience could understand.
items.note: Book example of jargon: specialised language used by a professional or interest group.

items.section: B · Meaning, change and varieties of language
items.example: The editor annotated the obsolete language in the seventeenth-century letters.
items.note: Exercise category for linguistic forms no longer used in present-day ordinary speech.

items.pt: articulado; capaz de se expressar com clareza
items.section: C · Expressing yourself and conversational idioms
items.example: Despite the difficult questions, she gave an articulate explanation of her research.
items.note: Describes clear expression of ideas; not exactly the same as eloquent or persuasive.

items.section: C · Expressing yourself and conversational idioms
items.example: His eloquent speech persuaded the panel to reconsider its decision.
items.note: Suggests fluent, expressive speech that can move or persuade listeners.

items.section: C · Expressing yourself and conversational idioms
items.example: Please provide a succinct summary of the study's main limitations.
items.note: Expresses ideas clearly in few words; brevity without loss of the essential point.

items.pt: a palavra exata; o termo mais apropriado
items.section: C · Expressing yourself and conversational idioms
items.example: She paused until she found the mot juste for the unexpectedly delicate situation.
items.note: Borrowed French expression for exactly the right word or phrase.

items.pt: incapaz de se expressar com clareza; pouco articulado
items.section: C · Expressing yourself and conversational idioms
items.example: He grew inarticulate when asked to explain the contradictions in his statement.
items.note: Opposite of articulate in the expressive sense; does not necessarily imply lack of intelligence.

items.pt: sem palavras; sem conseguir falar de surpresa ou emoção
items.section: C · Expressing yourself and conversational idioms
items.example: I was speechless when the committee announced the unexpected award.
items.note: Often temporary because of shock, anger or surprise, unlike generally being inarticulate.

items.pt: sem palavras; sem saber o que dizer
items.section: C · Expressing yourself and conversational idioms
items.example: When the students thanked her publicly, the teacher was momentarily lost for words.
items.note: Idiom for being unable to find anything appropriate to say.

items.pt: cometer uma gafe; falar algo inconveniente
items.section: C · Expressing yourself and conversational idioms
items.example: I put my foot in it by congratulating him on a promotion he hadn't received.
items.note: Informal British-English idiom for accidentally saying something embarrassing or upsetting.
